note: wordPartClue is what the parts literally suggest. studentDefinition and scienceExplanation are the actual science meaning. They are kept separate on purpose: the clue opens the door, the science confirms the meaning.

terms.studentDefinition: The study of living things.
terms.scienceExplanation: Biology is the science of living things — how they are built, how they grow, what they need, and how they interact.
terms.contextExample: A biologist studying a pond records which plants and animals live there and what each one needs to survive.

terms.studentDefinition: The study of Earth and its rocks.
terms.scienceExplanation: Geology is the science of Earth's materials and the processes that change them, including rocks, soil, and the layers below the surface.
terms.contextExample: A geologist reads the layers in a canyon wall to work out which rock formed first.

terms.wordPartClue: home or surroundings + the study of
terms.studentDefinition: The study of how living things interact with their surroundings.
terms.scienceExplanation: Ecology examines the relationships between organisms and the living and nonliving parts of the place where they live.
terms.contextExample: Studying how a drought changes which animals stay in a prairie is ecology.

terms.studentDefinition: All of Earth's water.
terms.scienceExplanation: The hydrosphere is all the water on Earth — oceans, lakes, rivers, groundwater, ice, and water vapor in the air.
terms.contextExample: Oceans, lakes, groundwater, glaciers, and water vapor are all part of the hydrosphere.

terms.wordPartClue: vapor or air + region or layer
terms.studentDefinition: The layer of gases that surrounds Earth.
terms.scienceExplanation: The atmosphere is the mixture of gases held around Earth by gravity. It holds the air we breathe, carries weather, and blocks some of the Sun's energy.
terms.contextExample: Clouds form in the atmosphere when water vapor cools and condenses.

terms.studentDefinition: All the places on Earth where living things are found.
terms.scienceExplanation: The biosphere is every part of Earth where life exists, from deep ocean water to soil to the lower atmosphere.
terms.contextExample: Bacteria living in desert soil and fish living near the ocean floor are both part of the biosphere.

terms.studentDefinition: The rock and soil part of Earth.
terms.scienceExplanation: The geosphere is Earth's solid material — surface rock and soil, and the layers of rock and metal beneath.
terms.contextExample: A landslide moves material from one part of the geosphere to another.

terms.studentDefinition: A tool used to measure temperature.
terms.scienceExplanation: A thermometer measures temperature, which tells how hot or cold something is. Scientists use it to collect data they can compare.
terms.contextExample: Students used a thermometer to record the water temperature every ten minutes.

terms.studentDefinition: A tool that measures how fast something is moving.
terms.scienceExplanation: A speedometer reports speed — the distance an object travels in a certain amount of time.
terms.contextExample: The speedometer showed the car traveling 30 miles per hour.

terms.studentDefinition: A tool for looking at very small things.
terms.scienceExplanation: A microscope uses lenses to make small objects look larger, so scientists can observe details the eye cannot see alone.
terms.contextExample: Under a microscope, a drop of pond water is full of moving organisms.

terms.studentDefinition: A tool for looking at things that are very far away.
terms.scienceExplanation: A telescope gathers light from distant objects so they appear brighter and larger, which is how we observe planets and stars.
terms.contextExample: Through a telescope, the four largest moons of Jupiter look like tiny points of light in a line.

terms.studentDefinition: Too small to see without a microscope.
terms.scienceExplanation: Microscopic describes an object so small that a microscope is needed to observe it.
terms.contextExample: The leaf has microscopic openings that let gases move in and out.

terms.studentDefinition: Large enough to see without a microscope.
terms.scienceExplanation: Macroscopic describes something you can observe with your eyes alone.
terms.contextExample: The salt crystals were macroscopic, but the dissolved salt in the water was not visible at all.

terms.studentDefinition: The process plants use to make their own food using light.
terms.scienceExplanation: In photosynthesis, plants use energy from sunlight together with water and carbon dioxide to make sugar, and they release oxygen.
terms.contextExample: A plant kept in a dark closet for two weeks turns pale and stops growing well.

terms.wordPartClue: home or surroundings + parts working together
terms.studentDefinition: All the living and nonliving things in one place, working together.
terms.scienceExplanation: An ecosystem includes organisms and the nonliving parts of their environment — water, air, soil, sunlight — and the interactions among them.
terms.contextExample: A pond ecosystem includes fish, insects, algae, water, mud, and sunlight.

terms.studentDefinition: A living thing too small to see without a microscope.
terms.scienceExplanation: Microorganisms are organisms such as bacteria and many single-celled protists. They live in soil, water, air, and inside other organisms.
terms.contextExample: Microorganisms in the soil help break down fallen leaves.

terms.studentDefinition: An animal that eats plants.
terms.scienceExplanation: Herbivores are consumers that get their energy from producers. In a food chain, they usually come right after the plants.
terms.contextExample: A grasshopper eating grass is acting as a herbivore.

terms.studentDefinition: An animal that eats other animals.
terms.scienceExplanation: Carnivores are consumers that get their energy by eating other consumers. Energy in a food chain passes to them from the animals they eat.
terms.contextExample: A snake that eats frogs is a carnivore.

parts.meaning: a small animal with six legs

terms.studentDefinition: An animal that eats insects.
terms.scienceExplanation: Insectivores are a kind of carnivore. Naming what an animal eats helps explain its place in a food web.
terms.contextExample: A bat that catches moths at night is an insectivore.

terms.studentDefinition: A natural shape or feature of Earth's surface.
terms.scienceExplanation: Landforms such as mountains, valleys, canyons, and deltas are shaped over time by processes including weathering, erosion, and deposition.
terms.contextExample: A river slows near the coast and drops sediment, building a delta — a landform made by moving water.

terms.studentDefinition: To change from one form into another.
terms.scienceExplanation: In science, energy transforms from one form to another — for example, electrical energy transforms into light and thermal energy in a bulb.
terms.contextExample: When the bulb lights up, electrical energy transforms into light energy and thermal energy.

terms.studentDefinition: The same all the way through.
terms.scienceExplanation: Uniform describes something that does not vary — a uniform mixture looks the same in every sample you take from it.
terms.contextExample: After stirring, the salt water looked uniform — no grains settled at the bottom.

terms.studentDefinition: Heat that comes from inside Earth.
terms.scienceExplanation: Geothermal energy is thermal energy stored in Earth's interior. It heats underground rock and water, and in some places it can be used to warm buildings or generate electricity.
terms.contextExample: In Iceland, hot water from underground is piped into homes for heating.

terms.studentDefinition: Electricity made by moving water.
terms.scienceExplanation: In a hydroelectric plant, falling or flowing water turns a turbine, and that motion is used to generate electricity. It is a renewable resource.
terms.contextExample: Water released from behind a dam spins turbines that generate hydroelectric power.

terms.studentDefinition: To use a material again instead of throwing it away.
terms.scienceExplanation: Recycling returns materials such as aluminum, glass, and paper to be processed and used again, which conserves natural resources.
terms.contextExample: The class recycled aluminum cans so the metal could be melted and shaped into something new.

terms.studentDefinition: The continuous movement of water on Earth.
terms.scienceExplanation: Energy from the Sun drives evaporation. Water vapor rises, cools, and condenses into clouds, then returns to the surface as precipitation, and the pattern repeats.
terms.contextExample: A puddle shrinks on a sunny day. Later, clouds form and rain falls nearby.

terms.studentDefinition: The stages a living thing goes through from beginning to adult.
terms.scienceExplanation: A life cycle describes the sequence of stages an organism passes through, and it repeats when the adult produces offspring.
terms.contextExample: The life cycle of a butterfly moves from egg to larva to pupa to adult.

terms.studentDefinition: A resource that can be replaced in a short time.
terms.scienceExplanation: Renewable resources such as sunlight, wind, and moving water are replenished naturally on a human timescale. Nonrenewable resources such as coal are not.
terms.contextExample: A town compares a wind farm with a natural-gas plant and notes that only one uses a renewable resource.

terms.studentDefinition: Made of many cells.
terms.scienceExplanation: Multicellular organisms are built from many cells that work together, often with different cells doing different jobs.
terms.contextExample: An oak tree is multicellular: its leaf cells, root cells, and stem cells do different jobs.

terms.studentDefinition: Made of only one cell.
terms.scienceExplanation: A unicellular organism carries out all its life processes inside a single cell.
terms.contextExample: Many of the tiny moving organisms in pond water are unicellular.

terms.studentDefinition: In the form of a gas.
terms.scienceExplanation: Gaseous names one state of matter. In the gaseous state, particles are far apart and the material has no fixed shape or volume.
terms.contextExample: When water boils, liquid water becomes gaseous water vapor.

terms.studentDefinition: The layer of soil under the topsoil.
terms.scienceExplanation: Subsoil sits beneath topsoil. It usually holds less decayed plant material and more clay or small rock pieces.
terms.contextExample: The soil sample showed dark topsoil above a lighter, rockier subsoil.

terms.studentDefinition: Having to do with flight in the air and in space.
terms.scienceExplanation: Aerospace covers engineering and science for vehicles that travel through the atmosphere and beyond it.
terms.contextExample: An aerospace engineer tests how a model rocket moves through air before it leaves the atmosphere.

terms.studentDefinition: The study of objects in space.
terms.scienceExplanation: Astronomy studies the Sun, Moon, planets, stars, and their patterns of motion.
terms.contextExample: Recording the Moon's shape every night for a month is doing astronomy.

terms.studentDefinition: To say what you think will happen before it happens.
terms.scienceExplanation: A scientific prediction is based on evidence and on patterns you have already observed, not on a guess.
terms.contextExample: After watching shadows shrink all morning, students predicted the shortest shadow would come near noon.
